content: Having a healthcare worker visit a patient’s home regularly can sometimes lead to stigma and may create a sense of being watched over, which can be disempowering for patients. While treatment administered by a supportive relative or close friend may be more acceptable, it can still carry a stigma. Family members may not always be the best choice for supervising treatment due to complex family dynamics, and their suitability as treatment adherence supervisors must be carefully evaluated within each national or local context. If family members are already providing treatment support, they must be carefully identified and trained. Additional supervision by local supporters or healthcare workers is still necessary, as family members cannot be the sole option for care. Patients will continue to require social support even if family members are involved in treatment support. Healthcare workers must assess potential risk factors for poor adherence at the start of a patient’s treatment to determine the most appropriate treatment administration option. Certain groups of patients who are less likely to adhere to treatment may benefit more from treatment support than others. Additionally, some patients with inflexible work or family responsibilities may not be able to provide treatment support. Any treatment administration option offered to a patient must be accompanied by proper medical care, including regular pick-up of tuberculosis (TB) drugs, consultations with physicians or other healthcare workers when necessary, free TB treatment, and the provision of essential information about TB treatment. Monitoring and evaluation programs should measure whether providing incentives improves program performance. Patients with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) should primarily be treated using ambulatory care rather than hospitalization-based models. A decentralized model of care is recommended over a centralized model for patients on MDR-TB treatment. Observational studies comparing clinic-based ambulatory treatment with hospital-based inpatient treatment showed that the evidence was of very low quality due to the lack of randomized controlled trials. Cost-effectiveness modeling across various settings indicated that decentralized care is a practical approach for scaling up treatment and care for MDR-TB patients. Decentralized care, defined as care provided in the local community where the patient lives, involves non-specialized or peripheral health centers, community health workers, nurses, non-specialized doctors, community volunteers, or treatment supporters. Care can also occur at local venues, the patient’s home, or workplace. Treatment and care include patient support and injections during the intensive phase. A brief hospitalization phase of less than one month may be necessary for patients requiring it during the initial treatment phase or when complications arise. Centralized care, on the other hand, involves inpatient treatment provided solely by specialized centers or teams for the duration of the intensive therapy phase or until culture or smear conversion. Data analysis showed that treatment success and follow-up improved with decentralized care compared to centralized care, although the risk of death and treatment failure showed minimal differences. There was limited data on adverse reactions, adherence, acquired drug resistance, and cost. Both HIV-negative and HIV-positive individuals were included in the studies, but the data was not stratified by HIV status. Concerns were raised about potential bias, as healthcare workers may have selected patients with worse prognoses for centralized care. Decentralized care may not be suitable for patients with severe TB disease, highly infectious forms, serious comorbidities, or adherence concerns. Safety measures for MDR-TB regimens, especially those containing new or novel medicines, must be maintained in outpatient settings. Hospitalization should remain an option when appropriate. Ambulatory care costs varied widely across modeled settings, but in most cases, outpatient-based care was more cost-effective than inpatient-based care. The financial benefits of decentralized care include earlier treatment initiation, reduced resource use, and prevention of severe illness requiring more intensive medical care. However, infection control measures must be in place to reduce transmission risks in households, communities, and clinics. TB control programs must consider reallocating resources from hospital care to ambulatory care to implement necessary changes in patient management. Decentralized care for MDR-TB patients requires appropriate treatment supervision, patient education, social support, staff training, infection control practices, and quality assurance. National TB programs should have standardized guidelines for determining patient eligibility for decentralized care. Patient preference should be highly valued when choosing between centralized and decentralized care. The implementation of decentralized care may face legal barriers in some regions, particularly when treatment involves injections. These legal concerns must be addressed. For children and adolescents exposed to or diagnosed with TB, decentralized and family-centered care models are recommended to improve case detection and TB preventive treatment (TPT) provision. Pediatric TB care is often centralized at secondary or tertiary levels, leading to delays in accessing care. Primary healthcare workers may lack the capacity and confidence to manage pediatric TB, even though this is where most children seek care. TB screening is often not systematically integrated into child health clinical algorithms. Private-sector providers play an increasing role as the first point of care in many countries, but weak integration of child and adolescent TB services with other programs leads to missed opportunities for prevention, detection, and care. Decentralization and family-centered, integrated care are key actions highlighted in the 2018 Roadmap towards ending TB in children and adolescents. Addressing gaps and bottlenecks along the care continuum can reduce TB transmission, expand prevention, and enable earlier diagnosis with better outcomes. Achieving this requires collaboration across service areas, disciplines, and sectors, as well as community engagement and integration of service delivery at the primary healthcare level.
